clinical_category: Cor pulmonale - pulmonary hypertension causing right-ventricular adaptation and failure
blueprint_topic: Cardiopulmonary physiologic adaptation to chronic lung disease
stem: A client with advanced COPD develops pulmonary hypertension, jugular venous distention, and peripheral edema. Which pathophysiologic process best explains cor pulmonale in this client?

options.A: Chronic pulmonary vascular resistance increases right-ventricular workload, causing right-ventricular structural and functional change that may progress to right-sided failure
options.B: Primary left-ventricular systolic failure alone directly defines cor pulmonale
options.C: Pulmonary hypertension reduces right-ventricular afterload and progressively improves right-ventricular function
options.D: Cor pulmonale results from isolated systemic hypertension without a respiratory or pulmonary vascular disorder

rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance defines cor pulmonale as alteration in right-ventricular structure and function caused by a primary respiratory-system disorder that produces pulmonary hypertension. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance raises pulmonary arterial pressure and right-ventricular workload; with persistent high afterload, the right ventricle adapts and may eventually fail. B is incorrect because right-sided failure caused by left-sided heart failure is not classified as cor pulmonale in the cited definition. C reverses the hemodynamic effect of pulmonary hypertension. D omits the pulmonary disease/pulmonary-hypertension mechanism central to cor pulmonale.
educational_objective: Explain cor pulmonale as right-ventricular structural and functional deterioration caused by pulmonary hypertension and sustained right-ventricular afterload from underlying respiratory disease.
source_document_title: Cor Pulmonale; Pulmonary Hypertension Due to Lung Disease or Hypoxia
source_version_date: Cor Pulmonale last updated 2023-08-08; Pulmonary Hypertension Due to Lung Disease or Hypoxia last updated 2023-06-11; current StatPearls 2026 Internet editions accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Cor Pulmonale' → Introduction: alteration in RV structure/function caused by a primary respiratory disorder resulting in pulmonary hypertension; right-sided failure from left-sided heart failure is not cor pulmonale. Pathophysiology: increased pulmonary vascular resistance raises pulmonary arterial pressure and RV workload, leading to RV enlargement. NCBI Bookshelf 'Pulmonary Hypertension Due to Lung Disease or Hypoxia' → Complications: chronically elevated pulmonary arterial pressure increases RV afterload; compensatory RV hypertrophy can progress to RV dysfunction/failure and cor pulmonale.
source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports pulmonary hypertension from respiratory disease increasing right-ventricular afterload, producing structural/functional RV change and eventual right-sided failure, while excluding left-heart-failure-mediated right-sided failure from the cor-pulmonale definition.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation client-needs subcategory (11–17% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests understanding of cardiopulmonary consequences of chronic respiratory disease.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The generic ACC homepage was replaced with exact NCBI/StatPearls cor-pulmonale and group-3 pulmonary-hypertension locators. The final item tests the directly supported RV-afterload mechanism and explicitly excludes left-heart-failure-mediated right-sided failure, avoiding vague statements about an undefined cardiac complication.
audit_findings: The original ACC root URL did not provide an exact cor-pulmonale pathophysiology locator.
NCBI/StatPearls directly defines cor pulmonale through pulmonary-hypertension-mediated right-ventricular structural and functional change from respiratory disease.
The pathophysiology locator directly supports increased PVR, increased pulmonary arterial pressure, increased RV workload, and eventual RV failure.
The final item avoids unsupported universal timing or pulmonary-pressure thresholds and does not equate all right-sided heart failure with cor pulmonale.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct mechanism, no second defensible option, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
